content: Trichotillomania, also known as trichotillosis or compulsive hair pulling, is a condition characterized by hair loss resulting from repeated urges to pull or twist the hair until it breaks off. Patients with this condition are unable to stop this behavior, even as their hair becomes noticeably thinner. Symptoms of Trichotillomania: Symptoms typically begin before the age of 17. Hair may be pulled out in round patches or diffusely across the scalp, leading to an uneven appearance. Individuals may also pluck hair from other areas, such as the eyebrows, eyelashes, or body hair. Common symptoms observed in children include: Uneven hair appearance. Bare patches or diffuse hair loss. Bowel obstruction if the pulled-out hair is ingested (a condition known as trichophagia). Persistent tugging, pulling, or twisting of hair. Denial of hair-pulling behavior. Regrowth of hair in bare spots that feels like stubble. An increasing sense of tension before pulling hair. Engagement in other self-injurious behaviors. A sense of relief, pleasure, or gratification after pulling hair. Many individuals with trichotillomania also experience: Feelings of sadness or depression. Anxiety. Poor self-image. Causes of Trichotillomania: Trichotillomania is classified as an impulsive control disorder. The exact causes are not well understood. It may affect up to 4% of the population, with women being four times more likely to be affected than men. Diagnosis: Individuals with this disorder often first consult a dermatologist due to concerns about hair loss. A biopsy may be performed to rule out other causes of hair loss, such as scalp infections. Treatment Options: There is no consensus among experts regarding the use of medication for treatment. However, medications such as naltrexone and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have shown effectiveness in reducing some symptoms. Behavioral therapy and habit reversal training may also be effective treatment approaches. Prognosis: Trichotillomania that begins in younger children (under six years old) may resolve without treatment, with hair-pulling behavior often ceasing within 12 months. For others, trichotillomania can become a lifelong disorder. Treatment often improves hair-pulling behavior as well as associated feelings of depression, anxiety, or poor self-image. Possible Complications: Complications can arise if individuals ingest the pulled-out hair (trichophagia), which may lead to intestinal blockages or poor nutrition. Prevention: Early detection is the most effective form of prevention, as it allows for early intervention and treatment. Reducing stress levels can help, as stress may exacerbate compulsive behaviors.
